title: Sandtable Beacon
tagline: Throw a puck into the smoke: it ranges the phones of the people trapped inside, the building's twin turns rings into positions, and the tenant roster says who is still missing.
abstract: Beacon is the headline mode of Sandtable, the incident-command board for fire crews. A crew throws small UWB pucks (Qorvo DWM3001CDK boards) into a smoke-filled room. An occupant who opened the Beacon app on their iPhone is ranged by every puck over ultra-wideband, through Apple's Nearby Interaction accessory protocol, and the app sends a status with it: how many people, whether they can move, battery, floor. A locator fuses the ranges with the 3D twin's walls and is honest about geometry: one puck gives a ring, two give two candidates, the twin's walls or a third puck give a position. The building record's tenant roster is compared with the phones still inside, so the command agent gets an accountability table, search priorities and a report. Without the app a puck host can only count nearby Bluetooth devices, with no identities. Simulated end to end so far; the hardware path is written for tonight.
aha: A ring appears around the first puck: a trapped person's iPhone. The second puck, dropped carelessly, leaves two possible spots and the board says it cannot choose. Slide that puck to the wall and one spot falls outside the room: a position, and the tenant roster says how many people should still be in that suite.

left_hardware: 1. (5 min) Power one DWM3001CDK from USB. Install Qorvo's free 'Qorvo Nearby Interaction' app from the App Store on the iPhone 14 and see whether the board already shows up and ranges. If it does, that board needs no flashing.

2. (15 to 30 min, once) Get the firmware: Qorvo 'Nearby Interaction' package for the DWM3001CDK (file DWM3001CDK-QANI-FreeRTOS_full_QNI_3_0_0.hex, or the QANI hex inside the DW3_QM33 SDK) from qorvo.com/products/d/da008212 or /da008582. It is an email form; a work or school address works better than Gmail. Keep the .hex outside the repository folder.

3. (10 min per board) Flash through the on-board J-Link: micro-USB DATA cable into port J9, SEGGER J-Flash Lite (free, segger.com), device NRF52833_XXAA, erase, program, reset. Guide: hardware/FLASH.md (being written).
4. (5 min per board) Prove each board with Qorvo's app: distance on the phone, check it against a tape measure at 1 m and 3 m.

5. (20 to 40 min) Build our app: open apps/ios/SandtableBeacon.xcodeproj in Xcode, choose your team, run on the iPhone 14, then the iPhone 15. Guide: docs/IOS_BUILD.md (being written). If it does not compile, paste the errors back.

6. (10 min) Network: open a hotspot on the Android phone; join it with the laptop and both iPhones. On the laptop: `bash run_demo.sh --source live --lan` (Windows: see README). Open the board, scan its QR code with each iPhone's camera to fill in the server address.

7. (10 min) Pucks: puck A on a battery bank beside the UNO Q, puck B on the Android phone through a USB-OTG adapter into the board's J-Link port (J9). Stand both upright, 15 cm or more off the floor, component-free side toward the room. Both just inside the 'door wall' of your taped room, about 4 m apart in building metres (hardware/BRINGUP.md gives the taped-rectangle distances).
8. (5 min) On the board, click each puck onto the plan where it stands and set the exercise scale. Press a status button in the app on the iPhone 14: a ring, then a position.

9. (15 min) Second victim: iPhone 15. Switch 'Take turns' on in the app on both phones (the stock firmware serves one phone per board), or power two more boards so each puck position has one board per phone.
10. (10 min) Rehearse the two-minute run-through and the fallback ladder in hardware/BRINGUP.md.

owner_questions.q: Can a UWB board range a victim's phone over UWB at all?
owner_questions.a: Yes, with exactly your boards: a Qorvo DWM3001CDK running Qorvo's stock Nearby Interaction firmware ranges an iPhone 11 or later through Apple's accessory protocol, once the person has opened our app. Both your iPhones give distance (about 60 readings a second); neither gives direction to an accessory. The app reads the distance and reports it; the board itself only logs it on its debug channel.

owner_questions.q: Can it be done cold, to a phone whose owner installed nothing?
owner_questions.a: No. An iPhone's UWB radio only answers a session started by an app with the user's permission. Cold, a radio can only count Bluetooth advertisements nearby: a rough band of devices by signal strength, no identity, and devices are not people. The stock puck firmware cannot even do that; the UNO Q's own radio can (written, never run).

owner_questions.q: One puck or two for angle?
owner_questions.a: Two pucks, as you chose, give one answer if you place them right. One puck gives a ring; two give two mirror spots across the line between the pucks. Put both pucks just inside the wall the door is in (35 cm inside, about 4 m apart). Simulated over 800 phone positions in the room: one position in 77% of cases (48% by the twin's walls alone, 29% after the occupant's stated suite, shown as dismissed), median error 0.26 m, a wrong position in 1.1%; the rest stay a ring because only one puck reached the phone. Pucks dropped mid-room: one position in only 18%, and the board says 'cannot choose' in 57%. Better if you have it: a third puck gives one position in 88% with 0.20 m median error and no assumption. An iPhone 14 or 15 reports no direction to an accessory, so do not count on the phone's bearing.

owner_questions.q: Will the phone keep answering with the screen off?
owner_questions.a: Not as built tonight: keep the app open (it keeps the screen awake). Two ways exist and are not built: a Bluetooth-paired background session in which only the puck gets the measurements, and, on iOS 18.4 or later, a Live Activity that lets the app keep ranging.

owner_questions.q: Can we put both UWB boards on one device we throw in?
owner_questions.a: It works poorly. The boards have one antenna each, so bearing can only come from the difference of two ranges. Simulated: at 10, 30 and 50 cm spacing the bearing error is 22, 17 and 14 degrees (median), the sideways error 1.7, 1.3 and 1.3 m, the mirror ambiguity always remains, and the locator never publishes a position, only a ring. Two separate pucks 3 m apart: 5 degrees and 0.38 m sideways.

owner_questions.q: Two pucks: one on a battery bank with the UNO Q, one powered by the Android phone?
owner_questions.a: Yes, that is now the plan. Each board needs only 5 V. Puck A: battery bank, beside the UNO Q (which can run the server). Puck B: the Android phone over a USB-OTG adapter into the board's J-Link port (that port's chip shows up as a USB device, so the phone keeps the power on); keep a second bank as the fallback because some phones cut power to quiet devices. The phone cannot read the board (the stock firmware prints nothing on serial), and does not need to: the range returns through the iPhone app. The same phone can be the Wi-Fi hotspot for the laptop and both iPhones.

Power only (5 V on either micro-USB port). The range comes back through the iPhone app over Wi-Fi. Stand the board upright, at least 15 cm off the floor, component-free side toward the phone. Puck positions are measured with a tape and clicked onto the plan: the stock firmware cannot range board to board.

owner_questions.q: Two victims' iPhones on two pucks at once?
owner_questions.a: One iPhone can range both pucks at once. One board, on Qorvo's stock firmware, serves only one phone at a time (forum reports). So for two victims either the phones take turns (a switch in our app: each phone ranges a board for about 4 seconds and releases it; untested), or each puck position carries two boards, one per phone (you have five boards; continuous ranging, no turn-taking). Prove one phone on both pucks first.

owner_questions.q: Where does the server run at the table, and how do the iPhones reach it?
owner_questions.a: On the laptop, with the laptop and both iPhones joined to a phone hotspot (venue Wi-Fi usually blocks device-to-device traffic); the Android phone powering puck B can be that hotspot. The board shows a QR code; scanning it with the iPhone camera opens our app with the server address filled in. Fallbacks: the server on the UNO Q on the same hotspot, or this machine over the tailnet if the iPhones run the tailnet client.

limitations: Nothing has run on hardware. Every result is simulated, with the noise model stated next to it.
The iOS app is uncompiled Swift source (written on a machine with no Mac); expect compiler errors on the first build.
Qorvo's firmware is not in this repository and cannot be: the owner downloads it from Qorvo.
Bring-up guides are written from documentation and forum reports, not from a board.
With Qorvo's stock firmware one board serves one phone at a time, and the range is read by the phone app, not by the puck: the phone needs a network path to the server and the app must stay open.
An iPhone 14 or 15 reports distance but no direction to an accessory.
A phone whose owner installed nothing cannot be ranged or identified; at most a rough count of Bluetooth devices nearby.

The building record is a public-data fixture (not CoStar data) and the twin is a synthetic interior (not a Matterport scan); expected head counts are estimates from floor area and building-code load factors.
